source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) NDM-inspired prompts for care-seeking advice, JMIR Biomed Eng (full text, GPT-5.2 result)
finding: The RPD prompt gain did not replicate for GPT-5.2. The cause looks like a floor effect: GPT-5.2 almost never gave self-care advice under any prompt, and the gain in the other models came almost entirely from self-care cases.
numbers: 10 ChatGPT models, 3 prompts, 45 vignettes (2 emergency, 30 nonemergency, 13 self-care by subtraction), 10 repeats each. Self-care accuracy, default / RPD / data-frame: GPT-5.1 Instant 5.4 / 33.1 / 10.8; GPT-5.1 Thinking 16.9 / 36.2 / 34.6; GPT-5.2 Instant 0 / 3.1 / 0; GPT-5.2 Thinking 0.8 / 0 / 0.8. GPT-5.2 nonemergency: Instant 80 / 76.7 / 76.3; Thinking 71 / 73 / 70.7 (no gain).
quote: most nonreasoning models with NDM-inspired prompts outperformed traditional reasoning models using the default prompt
limits: Authors read it as a version-level shift to 'send to a professional' that prompting does not change. GPT-5.1 has the same reasoning design but did not show the drop, so it is not just the reasoning mechanism. This is the authors' reading, not a tested cause.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only keep-first-and-simulate step can fail when the base model has a strong prior. The gain is a shift of a default (over-caution), not better search. Test the prompt against a model's own bias before trusting it.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) full text: overall effects, variability and limitations
finding: The paper has no length-matched neutral prompt. The comparison is default (classify only) vs RPD prompt vs data-frame prompt, so extra reasoning text is not separated from the RPD content. The two NDM prompts scored nearly the same, which is also what a generic 'think first' effect would predict.
numbers: Overall accuracy 63.3 default, 67.6 RPD, 66.7 data-frame. Modal-answer consistency across 10 repeats: 76.9% default, 66.9% RPD, 71.1% data-frame (not significantly different, z=1.50). Gains appeared in reasoning models too (the authors' argument that it is not just added reasoning). Sensitivity test used temperature 0 on the 2 most-improved models; higher temperature was not used because models often refused.
limits: Single domain (care-seeking advice), only 2 emergency cases, ChatGPT-only models. The limitations section lists these but does not mention the missing neutral-prompt control.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays partly open: no other task, no other model family, no length-matched control. Treat the RPD-prompt gain as 'a structured think-first prompt helps on ambiguous triage', not as proof of RPD.

source: Lee et al. (2026) DART: Draft-Agreement Routing for Training-Free Adaptive Thinking Budgets (arXiv 2606.23181 v4)
finding: A training-free typicality gate works: sample two cheap no-think drafts, keep the answer if they agree, think only if they disagree. Agreement stands in for 'this case is typical enough to keep the first answer'.
numbers: Qwen3 8B/14B/32B plus DeepSeek-V3.2 on MATH-500, OlympiadBench, HumanEval, MBPP. Matches or beats always-think on 13 of 14 model-benchmark pairs; thinking tokens down 32 to 73%; up to +9.0 points on olympiad math and +22.5 on code. Qwen3-8B MATH-500: DART 88.2 vs always-think 85.6. Stage 1 answers directly for 78 to 82% of queries. Oracle router 91.2; DART captures 79% of the oracle gain over no-think 76.6.
limits: Error analysis, MATH-500: 59 errors, 36 (61%) are false accepts (drafts agree on a wrong answer), 23 are think-mode failures. False accepts had 1.38x higher draft entropy. Not valid for multiple choice (chance agreement is high). Math and code only. No head-to-head with Thinkless is reported; AdaptThink appears only in a related-work table.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 in part: answer consistency is a usable keep-first cue on open-answer tasks, and it is training-free. The main risk is confident agreement on a wrong answer, which is the RPD failure (a typical-looking but atypical case).

source: Lee et al. (2026) DART Table 2: self-prompted gates versus agreement gate and supervised routers (Qwen3-8B)
finding: Prompt-only self-assessed gates ('does this need thinking?') are weaker than the agreement gate. The model's own difficulty claim is not a reliable typicality signal.
numbers: Accuracy (token saving vs always-think) MATH-500 / OlympiadBench / HumanEval: MC-Binary (model asked if thinking is needed) 85.8 (4%) / 69.9 (0%) / 10.4; MC-Conf (self-reported confidence) 85.8 (24%) / 54.9 / 8.5; majority vote K=7 84.8 / 58.7 / 9.8; MLP router 81.0 / 58.2 / 62.5; DART 88.2 (35%) / 69.8 (9%) / 78.7 (52%). Always-think 85.6 / 71.5 / 59.1.
limits: One 8B model for this table. The HumanEval collapse of the vote and self-prompt rows is partly because text votes cannot compare code; the paper uses execution agreement for code.
agent_relevance: A prompt that asks the agent 'is this typical?' is a weak gate. Use observed signals (agreement of two cheap drafts, retrieval similarity) rather than self-report.

source: Ning et al. (2026) HRBench: thinking-mode switch strategies in hybrid-reasoning LLMs (arXiv 2605.28398)
finding: Controlled comparison of prompt-based, router-based and speculative (fast first, escalate on uncertainty) switching on 6 models and 5 benchmarks (527 runs). Training-free prompt switching was the best trade-off at some scales; speculative try-then-escalate gave the best accuracy at higher token cost. No strategy won at every scale.
numbers: Finding 1: prompt-based switch (PT-TF) is Pareto-optimal, higher accuracy than full-think with fewer tokens; on Qwen3.5-9B it gave the best accuracy with 24% token reduction, router 13% saving, speculative extra tokens. Finding 4: at 9B and 1.1T prompt-based leads (47.6 and 80.8); at 20B and 671B speculative leads (36.8 vs 32.9; 75.8 vs 74.7); at 2B all three are equal (13.2 to 14.1). Speculative with entropy trigger paid off most on code ('try-then-verify').
limits: Benchmarks are math, science, code with verifiable answers, not expert-labelled incident cases. Some table rows are shifted in the PDF text, so only the stated findings are quoted.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a prompt-only gate can match or beat trained routers at some scales, so Thinkless/Dualformer-style training is not required. Gap 6: an entropy or uncertainty trigger for escalation raises accuracy but costs tokens, and its value depends on model size.

source: Guo et al. (2026) Think When Needed: Model-Aware Reasoning Routing for LLM-based Ranking (SIGIR 2026, arXiv 2601.18146)
finding: On ranking tasks a Think mode costs about 8x the tokens of Non-Think and Non-Think wins on a substantial share of instances. Letting the LLM pick its own mode (Self-Select) stayed well below ideal routing and below the trained router.
numbers: Three public ranking datasets, several open-source model sizes. Think uses roughly 8x tokens vs Non-Think. Self-Select rows sit between Non-Think and Think and well under Ideal routing. The router head uses pre-generation features (candidate dispersion) and a model-aware checklist.
limits: Ranking, not decision-making or planning. I read the abstract, intro and result tables, not every ablation.
agent_relevance: A second source that the model's own 'should I think' self-selection is unreliable (gap 2). Candidate dispersion is a pre-generation typicality cue that needs no generation.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (arXiv 2310.01798)
finding: A check without outside feedback does not protect a first answer. With oracle labels the second look helps a lot; without them accuracy falls. This is the closest controlled test of 'keep first, then check by yourself' against 'keep first'.
numbers: Intrinsic self-correction, rounds 0/1/2: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 / 75.1 / 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 / 38.1 / 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 / 25.0 / 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 / 91.5 / 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 / 79.5 / 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 / 49.0 / 43.0. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, GPT-4 95.5 to 97.5. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; when it did change, it more often turned a right answer wrong.
limits: 2023 models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2). Reasoning models trained with RL may self-check better; this paper does not test them. Table cells in my text extraction are row-shifted, so the numbers follow the paper's text and column pattern.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: for LLMs, a same-model review or simulation step with no external check is not what protects the first option. In human RPD the protection comes from the expert's real model of the world. An agent needs an external check (a verifier, a test), not only a re-read.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) Can LLMs Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans? (arXiv 2310.08118)
finding: GPT-4 generating a plan and checking its own plan: the self-check was weak because the verifier approved plans that were wrong. An external sound verifier (VAL) gave the largest gain.
numbers: 100 planning instances (PDDL, Blocksworld-style). Generator alone, no backprompting: 40/100 valid. LLM generator plus LLM verifier with backprompting: 55/100 (3.48 iterations). LLM plus external verifier VAL: 88/100 (4.18 iterations). LLM verifier accuracy 61/100; it labelled 54 of 55 valid plans valid but also labelled 38 of 45 invalid plans valid (false-positive rate 84.45%). Binary vs detailed feedback made little difference.
limits: The abstract says self-critiquing 'appears to diminish' plan generation performance; that is relative to the external verifier, since 55 beats 40 in the table. One model (GPT-4, 2023), one domain.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and gap 1: the first-plan workable rate for GPT-4 here is 40%. The same-model check approves 84% of bad plans, so it cannot stand in for a real simulation. Use code, rules or a second source of information for the check step.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) Planning in Strawberry Fields: o1 on PlanBench (arXiv 2409.13373)
finding: First-attempt plan validity rates on a planning task with an automatic validator. These are the closest numbers to a 'first option workable rate' for models (not expert-labelled).
numbers: Blocksworld, 600 instances, zero-shot, plans valid: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 54.8%, Claude 3 Opus 59.3%, GPT-4o 35.5%, GPT-4o-mini 8.8%, GPT-4 34.6%, GPT-4 Turbo 40.1%, Llama 3.1 405B 62.6%, Llama 3 70B 34.2%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 23.8%. o1-preview 97.8%, o1-mini 56.6%, Fast Downward 100%. On obfuscated Mystery Blocksworld the standard models are near 0 to 5%.
limits: Blocksworld is a closed toy domain with a perfect validator. Expert-labelled incident cases are not tested. I could not read the Mystery and randomized rows cleanly from the PDF table, so no o1 figure is given for them.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly: model first-plan workable rates range from 9% to 98% on one validated domain, so keep-first is only safe where the measured rate is high. Measure it per task before using keep-first.

source: Gu et al. (2025) Is Your LLM Secretly a World Model of the Internet? WebDreamer (arXiv 2411.06559) ablation
finding: The only direct ablation found of 'simulate each option before committing' against 'just rank options' and 'no simulation'. Simulating the outcome of each candidate beat plain re-ranking and the reactive agent.
numbers: Success rate (%) on VisualWebArena / Online-Mind2Web / Mind2Web-Live: reactive 17.6 / 26.0 / 20.2; tree search 26.2 / n.a. / n.a.; WebDreamer (GPT-4o world model) 23.6 / 37.0 / 25.0 (relative +34.1%, +42.3%, +23.8%). Ablation on the VWA shopping human subset (read from a figure): reactive 21.1, reranking without simulation 22.8, without self-refinement 27.2, full WebDreamer 29.8. Action steps about equal to reactive; 4 to 5 times more efficient than tree search.
limits: Compares one-step simulation of several candidates, so it is generate-N-then-simulate, not keep-first. One subset; figure values are read off a chart.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: shows simulation adds value beyond ranking in a web task with an LLM world model. It does not test keep-first-with-simulate against N-and-compare at equal tokens (gap 1 stays open).

source: Yin, Vardi, Choudhary (2025) Fragile Preferences: order effects in LLMs (arXiv 2506.14092 v2)
finding: The first-position effect depends on quality. When options are good, models favour the first one; when options are poor, they favour later ones. So 'first option is the best' is not a stable property of LLM option lists.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3 Haiku, Llama 3 8B (Claude 4 Sonnet in one appendix). Pairwise share choosing the first-listed option (T=1), colors Ideal / Fair / Plain / Harsh: GPT-4o-mini 98 / 89 / 31 / 21; Claude 3 Haiku 73 / 15 / 20 / 15; Llama 3 8B 72 / 86 / 60 / 16; Claude 4 Sonnet 91 / 16 / 4 / 2. Resumes Best / Good / Mediocre / Weak: GPT-4o-mini 100 / 23 / 3 / 0. Triplewise Harsh: GPT-4o-mini 5 / 31 / 64 for positions 1 / 2 / 3. At T=0 GPT-4o-mini always chose the middle option for Plain colors.
limits: This is the order of presentation in a given list, not the order in which a model generates its own options. No reasoning models tested, so gap 5 on reasoning vs non-reasoning stays open. Small models, two domains.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly: there is no direct test of option quality by generation order. What exists is position bias that flips with quality, and at T=0 it is hidden. A keep-first agent must not rely on the model's list order.

source: Pezeshkpour & Hruschka (2024, Findings NAACL) Large Language Models Sensitivity to The Order of Options in Multiple-Choice Questions (arXiv 2308.11483)
finding: Reordering answer options changes accuracy by a large amount. The effect is strongest when the model is unsure between its top 2 or 3 choices.
numbers: Performance gap of about 13% to 75% across benchmarks when options are reordered, also with few-shot demonstrations. Calibration methods gave back up to 8 percentage points. Placing the top two choices first and last amplifies bias; placing them adjacent reduces it.
limits: Multiple choice with fixed options, models from 2023. Not about the order in which a model produces options.
agent_relevance: If a verifier or the agent picks among options, shuffle the order and check agreement, or the first-listed option gets an unearned boost.

source: Hassid et al. (2026, v2) Don't Overthink it: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains (arXiv 2505.17813)
finding: Within one question, the shortest (earliest finished) chain is more often right than a random or the longest one. Taking the first m chains that finish (short-m@k) beat majority voting at low compute. This is a generate-several, keep-the-quick-one test of 'first is good'.
numbers: Four reasoning LLMs, four benchmarks. Shortest chain beat a random chain by up to 18.8 points and the longest chain by up to 34.5 points. The shortest chains are 50% and 67% shorter than random and longest. short-1@k matches or beats majority voting with up to 40% fewer thinking tokens; short-3@k beats majority at all budgets and cuts wall time by up to 33%.
limits: Math and similar verifiable tasks. 'Shortest' is not 'first generated', but the logic (stop at first finish) is close. Fine-tuning on short chains also helped.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly: on verifiable reasoning tasks early-finishing answers are good, so keep-first-finished is competitive with compare-N at equal or lower tokens. Not shown for planning or expert-labelled cases.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking (Apple; arXiv 2506.06941 v3)
finding: Three regimes by task complexity at equal inference compute: on low-complexity puzzles non-thinking models beat reasoning models; at medium complexity thinking helps; at high complexity both collapse. In simple cases the correct answer shows up early in the trace and later alternatives are mostly wrong.
numbers: Puzzles with a simulator (Tower of Hanoi and others), Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking traces. Tower of Hanoi N=1 to 4: accuracy of intermediate solutions falls with position in the trace (overthinking). N=5 to 7: slight rise with continued reasoning. N>=8: near-zero accuracy. At high complexity models fixate on early wrong attempts and effort drops even with spare budget.
limits: Puzzle environments, not human-expert domains. The paper has been contested by critiques that blame output-length limits for part of the collapse; I did not open those.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: task complexity is a real moderator of keep-first. Keep-first fits the low regime and fails in the high regime. Matches Moxley et al. (chess: first move held on easy positions).

source: Chen et al. (2025, ICML) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-like LLMs (arXiv 2412.21187)
finding: On easy items the first solution round is usually enough. Later rounds add tokens and almost no accuracy. Shortening to the first correct round kept accuracy.
numbers: For 'what is 2 plus 3', o1-like models used on average 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. In more than 92% of cases (among responses that reach a correct answer) the first solution round already holds the correct answer, using under 60% of the tokens; QwQ-32B-Preview on ASDIV first round averages 287 tokens, 38.7% of the response. Overthinking is more frequent on easy sets (ASDIV < GSM8K < MATH500).
limits: The 92% is conditional on the response containing a correct solution, so it does not say how often the first solution is right overall. Math sets only; QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 5: strong evidence that the first solution is usually worth keeping on easy items. It does not say how to detect an easy item before spending tokens.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency (arXiv 2305.11860)
finding: A stopping rule for sampling: stop as soon as the leading answer is clearly ahead (Dirichlet model of the vote). A cheap drop-the-first-option trigger is 'the early samples disagree'.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, 3 LLMs. Sample budget cut by up to 7.9 times with average accuracy drop below 0.1% (0.07% in the table).
limits: Answers 'how fast should it fire' only in samples, not for plan-level mismatch events. Needs several samples per query.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: agreement across a handful of cheap samples is a well-tested trigger for keep versus escalate. The founding RPD study had only 3 of 156 mismatch events, so a rare-event trigger is a different problem from a vote.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024, NeurIPS) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: chess scaling analysis (arXiv 2402.04494)
finding: Case memory has to be large before recognition replaces search. Accuracy rose with training-set size at every model size, and larger models overfit when the set was small. Memorisation did not explain it.
numbers: Training sets of 10K, 100K and 1M games in the scaling study. Models of 7M parameters or more overfit at 10K games; the overfit disappears at 100K and 1M. Final puzzle accuracy rises with dataset size at every model size. Less than 1.41% of the initial puzzle board states appear in training.
limits: Chess, a closed game with exact labels from Stockfish. The paper gives no clean 'games needed to replace search' threshold. Not a text-case-memory result.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open for text agents: this shows a data-scale dependence for a trained policy, not for retrieval over cases. No study found measures the case count at which keep-first matches search.

source: Search record, gap search for E12.06 (2026-11-01)
finding: Gaps 8 and 9 and most of 7 stayed open. The shared web-search quota ran out and arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar answered 429 to later queries, so no new papers were found on: Army single-course-of-action versus three-course comparison with blind-scored outcomes, red-team adversary best reply under keep-first, and token caps in LLM chess.
numbers: Searches that worked: 3 WebSearch queries (Kopka, option-order bias, adaptive-thinking routers). Searches that returned 429: arXiv API, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, arXiv listing pages.
limits: Absence here is a limit of the search, not evidence that the studies do not exist.
agent_relevance: Do not treat gaps 7, 8, 9 as answered. The prior evidence in a19 (self-estimated 30% time saving; Thunholm 20% faster tempo) is still the best on gap 8.
